title: Outcome-Anchored Credit Reallocation for Agentic Knowledge Graph Question Answering
authors: Mingyuan Li, Yucheng Li, Xiaxia Wang et al.
abstract: Agentic knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to solve complex questions through multi-turn interactions with a knowledge graph (KG). title: Bridging Concepts: Multi-Agent Reasoning over Scientific Concept Graphs for High-Impact Research Prediction
authors: Donggyu Yoon, Minsung Hwang, Juneha Baek et al.
abstract: Within a research community, new topics often emerge when previously unconnected concepts are first studied together. We construct scientific concept graphs (SCGs)--domain knowledge graphs whose nodes are fine-grained research concepts extracted from paper text by LLMs and whose edges capture their co-occurrence in papers--and study the task of forecasting high-impact concept pairs, i.e., discovering concept pairs that are currently unconnected but will have high impact when connected. title: Dialogue Generation for Conversational Recommendation Using User Search Interactions and Knowledge Graphs
authors: Minsung Hwang, Donggyu Yoon, Gowoon Hwang et al.
abstract: Large-scale conversational recommendation datasets typically require manual dialogue construction or annotation. We propose SearCl, which automatically generates conversational recommendation dialogues grounded in user search and click behaviors. SearCl segments user interactions into query sessions and derives each recommendation target from content selected after a search query. title: Indistinguishable Agents: Training Agent Privacy as Twin-World Indistinguishability
authors: Jiaming He, Guanyu Hou, Yi Yu et al.
abstract: LLM agents search, shop and send messages for their users, and every action is seen by some party. Existing privacy training rewards agents for not mentioning protected items, yet an observer can infer a private fact from what the agent does. Since an observer learns a fact only if its view changes with the fact, we propose \methodfull (\method), which trains on twin worlds that differ only in the private fact. title: Trackable Skill Library Lifecycle Management for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Xi Zhu, Yuanlin Duan, Changyi Yang et al.
abstract: Skill-augmented agentic RL has emerged as an effective approach to improving LLM agents on long-horizon tasks. Despite this progress, individual skills may follow distinct trajectories as the policy evolves, with some becoming redundant after the model internalizes their capabilities, others remaining valuable as external scaffolding, and still others turning harmful. title: Memories That Outlive Their Reasons: Dependency-Tethered Memory for Tool-Using LLM Agents
authors: Yiqi Wang, Jinqian Ju, Jiaqi Zhang et al.
abstract: Agents now act on the Web, publishing packages, models and datasets through registry APIs, and remembering past verifications spares them the work. But a verdict rests on premises. When a signing key is revoked, everything built on it stops passing, yet the advisory names only the key, and the old verdicts of its dependents may never share a retrieval window with it. title: Explore or Confirm? LLM Agents Misallocate Measurements Under Noise
authors: Abdul Karim, Matt Keon
abstract: As model reasoning gets cheaper, the physical experiment becomes the slow and costly step in discovery. Each experiment returns a noisy reading: a high value can mean a good candidate or a lucky draw. With a fixed budget, an AI agent must keep choosing between exploring a new candidate and confirming a promising one by re-testing it. title: LLM Agents as Suppliers of Physical System Models: Calibration and Acceptance in Modelica
authors: Jörg Frochte, Herbert Schmidt
abstract: To procure a model of a device, a client hands a supplier a description, sometimes with recorded data or a target response, and accepts the model against this handover. We let LLM coding agents act as the supplier on handovers with data, building Modelica models from library components for four simulated systems and a real switching magnet, and ask what acceptance certifies. title: CorrectRTL: Boost RTL Generation Quality Through Automated Self-Correction with Instruction Decomposition
authors: Jing Wang, Shang Liu, Hangan Zhou et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong promise in specification-to-RTL generation. Among the explorations, the self-correction paradigm has significantly advanced LLM-based RTL generation. However, two challenges limit further progress. Existing benchmarks are saturated by advanced LLMs, leaving little room to evaluate the agentic self-correction framework. title: MemPrice: Online Memory Allocation via Adaptive Pricing for Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Yiming Zong, Shiyuan Piao, Jiashuo Jiang et al.
abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents face a fundamental allocation problem as interaction histories grow: which information to retain, how much context to devote to it, and at what granularity. Existing memory mechanisms largely focus on relevance, retrieval, or compression, leaving this allocation trade-off implicit. title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
authors: Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Xuyu Wang
abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. title: ATEST: Adaptive Resource-Aware Test-Time Scaling for LLM Inference
authors: Mobina Kashaniyan, Ali Jannesari
abstract: Test-time scaling (TTS) improves large language model (LLM) reasoning by sampling multiple answers, but fixed sampling budgets ignore both query difficulty and the changing energy cost of inference under GPU contention. We measure up to a 4.1-fold increase in energy for the same four-sample query as GPU load rises. title: Formal Raising: Embedding Verifiable Ethical Properties into the Development of AI
authors: Rolf Drechsler, Christina Plump
abstract: Alan Turing proposed constructing a ``child machine'' and educating it rather than directly programming an adult-like intelligent machine. Recent work on model raising revives this developmental view for Large Language Models by arguing that moral values should accompany capability acquisition from the beginning rather than be added only through post-hoc alignment. title: System X: An LLM Decision Model That Replies from Its Own KV Cache
authors: Syed Usama Khalid Bukhari, Syed Safwan Khalid, Muhammad Aamir
abstract: Decision models return probabilities over supplied options, but a deployed agent may also need to reply in words. The present study introduces System X, a large language model (LLM) decision model that adds a text-reply option to the LLM-as-Jev readout. When this option wins, or confidence is low, the same model continues from the decision's key-value (KV) cache, avoiding a repeated prompt prefill. title: Stepwise Reasoning Verification: Don't Generate, Classify!
authors: Yifei Shi, Michalis Korakakis, Rami Aly et al.
abstract: Verifying the reasoning of large language models is increasingly important as they are applied to complex mathematical and scientific problems. Existing work focuses on large decoder models and reports mixed results for generative and discriminative verifiers, leaving unclear which paradigm is more effective and whether large models are necessary. In this work, we cast stepwise verification as a natural language inference task: the problem and partial solution prefix form the premise, while the

title: When Form Changes but Logic Doesn't: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Logical Structure
authors: Xuyuan Liu, Xinshuai Dong, Elynn Chen et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this performance reflects an understanding of underlying logical structure or a reliance on shallow semantic cues. A key indicator of such understanding is whether models treat logically equivalent inputs consistently, producing the same predictions despite differences in expression. title: From Unverifiable Domain Text to Cross-Lingual RLVR via Code-Switched Task Synthesis
authors: Cheonbok Park, Jihwan Kim, Shinyoung Joo et al.
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) can improve reasoning in large language models, but specialized non-English domains expose a data mismatch. Raw English domain text is often available, while target-language RLVR tasks with verifiable rewards are scarce. We introduce code-switched task synthesis for cross-lingual RLVR, a data-centric approach that derives target-language and code-switched RLVR task variants from otherwise unverifiable English domain text. title: Where and Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail When Reasoning over Rapidly Evolving Knowledge
authors: Tianyi Hu, Bhavyajeet Singh, Niket Tandon et al.
abstract: As the world changes, new information is published while older records remain online. This complicates reasoning for large language models (LLMs), which must retrieve evidence and resolve conflicts to determine which information remains valid. Existing evaluations treat information seeking as a black box, revealing little about where and why LLMs fail. title: Calibration-Free Early Stopping for Chain-of-Thought Reasoning via E-processes
authors: Dong-Jae Lee, Gyojin Han, Junmo Kim
abstract: Reasoning large language models (LLMs) benefit from test-time scaling, motivating adaptive policies that spend tokens when they help and stop early otherwise. Existing rules halt when a confidence or stability signal crosses a threshold, but such thresholds rarely transfer across models and datasets, and validation-calibrated rules lose their guarantee under shifts in test-time horizon or signal dynamics. title: TIRE: Top-Down Formula Instantiation with Reliable Execution for Physics Problem Synthesis
authors: Xiaoyu Wu, Zhaoxin Yu, Xinglin Xiao et al.
abstract: Advancing physics reasoning in large language models requires scalable training data that connect physical laws, concrete problem scenarios, and verifiable numerical answers. Expert-designed problems offer top-down control over physical laws, conditions, and scenarios, but require costly human effort. title: Beyond Factual Accuracy: A Benchmark for Evaluating Perspective Alignment in LLMs
authors: Sunghoon Kim, Sangyeop Kim
abstract: Large Language Models often generate factually correct responses that fail to maintain user-requested perspectives, blending multiple perspectives and forcing users to filter through unwanted information---a perspective control failure that factual accuracy metrics cannot detect. title: ReTrace: Visual Backtracking for Efficient Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Guangzong Si, Dong Wang, Yifan Yu et al.
abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) encode images into dense visual token sequences, creating substantial attention and KV-cache overhead. Existing visual token compression methods reduce this cost by pruning low-saliency tokens in shallow layers, but this practice couples temporary computational deactivation with irreversible information deletion. title: DeGMatch: Target-Aware Reasoning Data Selection via Deconfounded Gradient Matching
authors: Changho Lee, Janghoon Han, Rajdeep Mukherjee et al.
abstract: Reasoning post-training on long trajectories has substantially improved the reasoning capabilities of large language models, but scaling such training to large datasets is increasingly expensive. We study target-aware reasoning data selection, where a small reference set specifies a target capability and guides the selection of training trajectories for specialization. title: CasePlay: Self-Play Reinforcement Learning from Case Reports for Medical Reasoning
authors: Hao Wang, Zihan Wang, Kai Wu et al.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising way to improve the clinical reasoning abilities of large language models (LLMs), but current pipelines often rely on expert-labeled questions or costly synthetic-data generation. Meanwhile, the medical literature offers a wealth of high-quality unlabeled documents, including clinical case reports that trace the full clinical course from initial presentation to final treatment decisions. title: A failure of Imagination: VLMs fail to use visual representations for text, but self-distillation can help
authors: Shashwat Singh, He He, Tal Linzen
abstract: Vision-language (VL) models are typically built by fine-tuning a language model to attend to visual features in service of a Visual Question-Answering objective. We ask whether this alignment changes how language models represent text---especially on tasks where visualization would help, like geometry questions posed in words. title: ViCoR: Estimating Visual Necessity via Counterfactual Residuals for Multimodal Medical Data Selection
authors: Haotian Gan, Yudong Li, Xintian Li et al.
abstract: Medical vision-language models often exhibit hidden stratification, where high overall performance masks failures on subtle visual findings and overlapping clinical conditions. We trace this failure mode to modality imbalance during fine-tuning, where strong linguistic priors can suppress visually grounded learning and induce plausible but weakly grounded rationales. title: Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Models for Spatiotemporal Brain MRI Forecasting
authors: Antonio Scardace, Silvia Ingala, Sebastiano Battiato et al.
abstract: Spatiotemporal forecasting of 3D anatomical changes is a critical generative vision challenge for modeling Alzheimer's Disease (AD) progression. While brain MRI forecasting from single-modality data has advanced, other key complementary multimodal biomarkers remain underutilized. In this work, we propose the Multimodal-Conditioned Latent Diffusion Model (MC-LDM), a novel framework for patient-specific brain MRI synthesis. title: Quality-Controlled Reply and Summary Data for Post-Training Small Language Models in AI Call-Screening Agents
authors: Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj et al.
abstract: Small language models have improved to the point where a phone can plausibly screen its own calls, answering on an absent owner's behalf without sending call content off the device, a privacy-respecting alternative to cloud call handling. Realizing that promise takes a model that can do two things well: reply within the owner's authority during the call, and afterward tell the owner what happened and what needs attention. title: Aligning Cultural Behaviors in Arabic Language Models via Preferences
authors: Junhong Liang, Daniil Orel, Saeed Almheiri et al.
abstract: Arabic LLMs have improved rapidly, but aligning them with country-specific cultural behavioral preferences remains underexplored. Previous work has focused primarily on instruction-tuning for factual knowledge, overlooking nuanced cultural behaviors. We propose ArabPref, which to our knowledge is the first large-scale pan-Arab preference data set for the alignment of cultural behavior conditioned on the country. authors: Hans Peter Lyngsøe Raaschou-jensen, M. Onurcan Kaya, Desmond Elliott
abstract: Recent test-time scaling methods improve model performance by increasing inference-time compute. One practical form of this is parallel scaling, where a model samples multiple independent reasoning streams and aggregates their answers using methods like voting, reranking, or verification. While effective, this approach leaves the streams uncoordinated, and a discovery made in one rollout cannot influence any other. title: Hidden Cartographer: Hidden State Guided Data Selection for Dual Budgeted Instruction Tuning
authors: Zixuan Qin, Qi Qin, Erbo Li et al.
abstract: Given the high cost of expert annotation and limited fine-tuning resources, effective data selection from large unlabeled pools under strict budgets has become a crucial step in adapting LLMs to specialized domains. Existing label-dependent methods risk distorted selection when using pseudo-labels, while traditional active learning methods do not explicitly characterize instruction-tuning dynamics. title: PLANE: Plug-and-Play Fine-Grained Visual Experts for Hallucination Mitigation in Large Vision-Language Models
authors: Jianghao Yin, Lang Yu, Qianxi Yu et al.
abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) commonly suffer from hallucinations, which appear as fabricating non-existent objects or outputting incorrect attributes and spatial relationships in images. Previous works empirically indicate that CLIP-style vision encoders tend to focus on primary objects while ignoring image details, which is one of the causes of hallucinations. title: Robust Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Label-Flip Attacks
authors: Chenye Yang, Weiyu Xu, Lifeng Lai
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) is widely used for offline Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback. However, recent works have shown that DPO can be easily manipulated by adversarial preference label flip attacks, which are specifically designed to mislead the learner toward an attacker-chosen target policy. title: Local Evidence, Global Failure: Diagnosing Speech-Vision Temporal Composition in Audio-Visual Language Models
authors: Jaehong Myung, Seunghun Oh, Unsang Park
abstract: Audio-visual large language models (AV-LLMs) can fail at full-video speech-vision decisions even when useful visual evidence is locally recoverable. We introduce Temporal Evidence Decomposition (TED), a training-free diagnostic framework that separates local visual verification from speech-relative aggregation. title: Towards Human-AI Complementarity for AI Safety
authors: Sander Lanbo Shi, Miranda Anna Christ, Eric Modesitt et al.
abstract: Safely overseeing AI is increasingly challenging for the humans doing it, as they must evaluate longer and more complex outputs with every new model generation. To mitigate this challenge, we could leverage complementarity: where humans and models make different mistakes, combining their judgements could yield an oversight signal stronger than either produces alone. title: When Empathy Misses the Goal: A Benchmark for Goal Displacement in LLM Advice
authors: Dean Ariel, Guy Laban
abstract: Conversational large language models can respond with warmth and reassurance while failing to advance the user's stated goal. We conceptualize this failure as $\textbf{goal displacement}$, the substitution of persona-maintenance content for goal-relevant substance. title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
authors: Owen Bianchi, Samer Aslan, Ryunosuke Saito
abstract: How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. title: Mixture-of-Memories: Low-Overhead Language Modeling with Modular Knowledge Injection
authors: Yifan Lu, Rubin Wei, Ziyun Zou et al.
abstract: Large language models store substantial factual knowledge in their parameters, yet this knowledge is difficult to control, update, and reliably elicit at inference time. Existing memory-augmented approaches typically rely on a single auxiliary mechanism, such as retrieval, parameter updates, or neural memory, and therefore apply the same form of correction to tokens with very different knowledge demands. title: Towards Figurative Language Understanding in Moroccan Darija: An Evaluation of Large Language Models
authors: Jihad R'baiti, Youssef Hmamouche, Emmanuele Chersoni et al.
abstract: Figurative language remains a major challenge for Machine Translation (MT) systems, as the intended meaning of such expressions often goes beyond literal translation. Although recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) improved the translation of Arabic dialects, benchmark resources for evaluating figurative language translation in Moroccan Darija remain scarce. title: NeuroAct: Advancing EEG Analysis and Decoding via Dual-Loop Autonomous Research
authors: Wei Xiong, Jiangtong Li, Han Zhao et al.
abstract: EEG analysis and decoding underpin brain-computer interfaces, cognitive assessment, and sleep monitoring. Fixed pipelines and reward-driven search do not explicitly determine how signal structure, representations, predictor behavior, and training dynamics contribute to performance or generalization gaps, leaving intervention choice underdetermined. title: Acharya 2.0: An AI Tutor for Self-Learning Subjects in Hindi
authors: Shantipriya Parida, Debasish Dhal, Sonal Khosla et al.
abstract: Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. title: Reranking Answers of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
authors: Mikhail Salnikov, Hai Le, Olga Tsymboi et al.
abstract: Answering natural language questions over knowledge graph data is challenging due to the vast number of facts, which can be difficult to process and navigate. One potential solution for this issue is to use mined subgraphs related to the query, although this process still requires extracting these subgraphs. title: World Models, Trees and Foundation Models for Retail Forecasting: Evidence from Four Public Data Sets
authors: Karthik Iyer, Madan Dabbeeru
abstract: A retailer makes different decisions at different grains of the product, store and time hierarchy: store orders for an item in a store, supplier funding for an item across stores, category performance by store, and the financial plan for the chain. Which forecasting model to use depends on the grain. title: Do LLMs Reproduce the Age Gap in Loneliness? Evaluating Survey Simulation against European Survey Data
authors: Yuliya Li, Achim Rettinger, Dominik Beyer
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often used to simulate survey respondents, but matching survey averages does not establish accurate demographic differences. We test whether LLM outputs reproduce within-country age gaps in loneliness using the 2022 EU Loneliness Survey, comparing adults aged 18-34 and 65 or older in France, Italy, Poland, and Sweden. title: Morpheus: a fully local, defense-in-depth de-identification engine for Greek clinical text - a benchmark evaluation
authors: Filippos-Paschalis Rorris, Nikoleta Stanitsa, Tatiana Rorri et al.
abstract: Background and Objective: Clinical free text cannot leave the hospital without de-identification, yet no de-identification system or benchmark exists for Greek clinical text. We evaluated Morpheus, a fully local de-identification pipeline for Greek clinical documents, on 500 synthetic discharge summaries. title: Deep Fusion Memory: A Chunk-Level Parametric Memory for Large Language Models
authors: Rubin Wei, Siyuan Sun, Hao Sun et al.
abstract: Large language models need effective ways to acquire and use external knowledge beyond what they retain from pretraining. Continued pretraining risks catastrophic forgetting, while retrieval at inference time can add substantial overhead. External parametric memory avoids online retrieval, but constructing its training data requires extensive offline search, and output-level interpolation provides only shallow fusion. title: One Head Away from Language Confusion: Single Attention Heads Across Model Families
authors: Jiwon Jeong, Anjelo Jann Laroza, Chaewoon Yoon et al.
abstract: Large language models sometimes reply in an unexpected language, a failure known as language confusion. We ablate individual attention heads in 12 model checkpoints spanning seven model series, using FLORES-200 continuations in five languages and Language Confusion Benchmark (LCB) chat replies. title: Synergy-Aware Residual Flow Matching for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
authors: Jingrui Wu, Wangyun Dan
abstract: Predicting single-cell responses to genetic and chemical perturbations is important for understanding regulatory mechanisms and prioritizing therapeutic interventions. Existing methods have made progress by modeling perturbation-conditioned expression shifts with neural networks, graph priors, foundation-model representations, or distributional generative models. title: UpLoop: Upcycling Large Language Models with Gated Loop
authors: Tieyuan Chen, Huabin Liu, Yingtao Zhang et al.
abstract: Looped large language models trade parameter storage for recurrent computation, but most are trained from scratch. In practice, pretraining with looped depth is expensive, making post-training upcycling of a pretrained non-looped LLM an attractive alternative. We introduce \textbf{UpLoop}, a post-training recipe based on \emph{layer-wise} recurrence. title: UtoMe: Observation-Uncertainty-Guided Token Merging for Weather Foundation Models
authors: Yunbei Zhang, Janet Wang, Xi Xiao et al.
abstract: Weather transformers process dense reanalysis fields whose reliability varies across variables, locations, and weather regimes. Token merging can reduce computation, but feature similarity alone does not account for this heterogeneous input uncertainty. We introduce UtoMe, an observation-uncertainty-guided token merging framework that combines dynamics saliency with ensemble data assimilation spread as a relative input-reliability proxy. title: SoK: PIAtlas: Decomposing the Unbounded Prompt Injection Attack Space
authors: Stavros Damianakis, Konstantinos Psounis
abstract: Prompt injection is the dominant security risk for large-language-model (LLM) applications and agents, yet the field still lacks a coherent map of how these attacks are constructed. More than twenty public datasets describe prompt injection using incompatible vocabularies, often organized around delivery vector, attacker goal, or generation method. title: A Measurement Perspective on Benchmarking LLM-Generated Text Detectors using Item Response Theory
authors: Yanbin Zhao, Zhipeng Chen, Guangsheng Bao et al.
abstract: Benchmarking large language model (LLM)-generated text detectors commonly relies on aggregate detector-level metrics such as accuracy, F1 score, and AUC. Although useful for summarizing overall performance, these metrics provide limited insight into how benchmark composition shapes detector comparisons or which texts distinguish detectors with different response profiles. title: Rubrics Carry the Standard: Shapley Attribution for Checklist-Based LLM Judges
authors: Saeid Asgari, Rui Ying, Sara Malvar et al.
abstract: Checklist rubrics applied by large language model (LLM) judges have become a standard instrument for evaluating open-ended outputs and for rewarding them during training. Two assumptions surround this practice: that leniency or strictness is a property of the judge model, and that a rubric can be improved by asking a model to review it. title: EG-GRPO: Evidence-Guided Step-level Credit Assignment for Deep Search Agents
authors: Sijia Luo, Mengjie Gao, Yuxiao He et al.
abstract: LLM-based search agents demonstrate strong capabilities in long-horizon information seeking and reasoning, typically trained via reinforcement learning. However, existing approaches predominantly rely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, providing limited supervision for complex search and reasoning processes. authors: Yam Eitan, Gilad Yehudai, Haggai Maron
abstract: Hybrid architectures offer a promising approach to efficient language modeling by combining a small number of full-attention layers with a larger number of efficient sequence layers, such as sparse attention and recurrent layers. title: MemBubble: Benchmarking How Agent Memory Shapes LLM Response Diversity
authors: Jiajun Tan, Fei Sun, Xinyu Ma et al.
abstract: Memory serves as the core component of LLM-based agents, enabling personalized responses via extracting and using user preferences from past interactions. However, its use may reduce response diversity, thereby narrowing the range of information available to users. Existing evaluations rely largely on synthetic interactions and cover few memory systems, leaving the effects of memory on response diversity insufficiently evaluated in real-world scenarios. title: Dual-Slot: From Serial Loops to Parallel Slots in Language Models
authors: Yiqin Hao, Zitong Wang, Boyi Zeng et al.
abstract: Looped language models increase computational depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, offering a way to improve model quality without adding parameters. However, sequential dependencies between loop iterations increase autoregressive decoding latency. We introduce Dual-Slot, an architecture that reorganizes serial looped computation into parallel latent and prediction slots. title: P2N: Reusing Deep Representations for Greater Effective Depth
authors: Yiqin Hao, Boyi Zeng, Zitong Wang et al.
abstract: Mathematical problem solving and autonomous agents are increasingly important applications of language models, demanding stronger reasoning capabilities. Computational depth is a key resource for such reasoning, but adding model layers increases both training and inference costs, while test-time scaling incurs substantial additional inference computation. We introduce P2N (Previous to Next), which reuses the previous token's deep representations, already available during generation, to increase

title: SteadyThought: Mitigating LLM Under-Thinking via Thought-Level Preference Optimization
authors: Zhenyue Peng, Lin Yang, Jie Wang et al.
abstract: Flexible switching between reasoning trajectories (i.e., thought switching) has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs). However, existing models often switch excessively yet fail to sustain promising reasoning thoughts, a phenomenon termed "under-thinking". title: Conjugate Compilation: Self-Improving Agentic Co-Compilation for Speculative Decoding
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Rohan Mahapatra, Christopher Priebe et al.
abstract: As LLM adoption surges, scaling model serving requires unlocking stranded GPU capacity alongside deploying more GPUs. Speculative decoding brings two models into the serving process: a small draft model proposes tokens that a larger target model verifies. Yet compiling these models individually leaves their shared execution outside the compiler's optimization boundary. title: The Bottleneck Is Retrieval, Not Reading: Diagnosing Evidence-Based Generation with RAG for Long Context Question Answering
authors: Debopriyo Banerjee, Owais Aijaz, Ahmer Tabassum et al.
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is the dominant paradigm for grounding large language models in external corpora, but its similarity-driven, chunked pipeline has structural blind spots: it cannot anticipate which passages a question requires and discards document-level context that resolves cross-passage references. title: MAMath-Bench: Process-Aware and Robust Evaluation of Multimodal Multi-Agent Mathematical Reasoning
authors: Xinping Wang, Jie Ma, Rui Xing et al.
abstract: Mathematical reasoning is a fundamental capability for educational applications of Large Language Models (LLMs), where reliable problem solving requires not only correct answers but also coherent and verifiable reasoning processes. Multi-agent systems (MASs) have shown growing potential in this domain by leveraging collaboration and verification among multiple LLM agents. title: Industrial Agentic AI: LLM-Driven New-Generation Agents for Smart Manufacturing
authors: Lei Ren, Haiteng Wang, Shixiang Li et al.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are enabling agents to move beyond predefined workflows toward autonomous planning and execution, creating new opportunities for smart manufacturing. However, dynamic environments, complex physical constraints, and stringent reliability requirements hinder the direct deployment of general-purpose agents in smart manufacturing. title: LightCRS: Lightweight Multi-Domain Conversational Recommendation System
authors: He Ma, Lan You, Qiyang Wu et al.
abstract: Conversational recommender systems have recently adopted vision-language models to match user dialogue intents with multimodal product information. title: How Far Can the Gemma 4 Speech Encoder Go Without Changing Its Weights? Saudi and Gulf Arabic Speech Recognition with a Frozen and an Adapter-Augmented Encoder
authors: Amr Abdelkhalik
abstract: We study the 305M-parameter audio encoder shared by Gemma 4 and EmbeddingGemma 2 (identical except for its final projection) for Saudi and Gulf Arabic speech recognition, without changing any of its weights. A frozen system trains only a 22.6M-parameter CTC reader over a mix of encoder layers; an adapted system adds 3.1M low-rank adapter parameters, a 41.5M-parameter hybrid CTC/attention reader and joint decoding with a sub-word language model. title: A Cross-Domain Evaluation of Prompting Techniques for Large Language Models
authors: Kevin Krazius, Tim Schlippe, Paul Libbrecht
abstract: Prompt engineering has become a central mechanism for guiding the behavior of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a wide range of reasoning and language understanding tasks [1], [2]. However, existing studies frequently evaluate prompting techniques using different LLMs, datasets, or task settings, making direct comparisons across methods and domains difficult [3]. title: Trust the Edge, Doubt the Arrow: Auditing Validation Signals for Text-Mined Clinical Causal Knowledge Graphs
authors: Su Lan, Shicheng Zhou, Yiqi Wang et al.
abstract: Clinical causal retrieval-augmented generation systems increasingly use knowledge graphs (KGs) mined from notes, yet extracted assertions remain candidates that require audit for patient-level EHR support and direction. title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents
authors: Soyoung Yoon, Peiran Xu, Han Wang et al.
abstract: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. title: The One-Pixel of Reasoning: One Truthful Relation Is Enough to Mislead LLM Agents
authors: Jinwei Hu, Youcheng Sun, Yi Dong et al.
abstract: Can one sentence manipulate an agent's belief by targeting a single implicit warrant linking evidence to a conclusion? In this paper, we introduce the one-relation attack (ORA), a novel cognitive attack on this inferential relation. ORA localizes a critical implicit warrant and performs a one-relation intervention using a single source-grounded sentence that qualifies this warrant and steers the agent toward an incorrect belief. title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
authors: Adarsh Vatsa, William Eiers
abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. title: Pair-Aware Optimization: Coordinating Exploration and Refinement for Jailbreaking LLM Agents
authors: Juanyang Xu, Zheng Wang, Xingyu Zhao et al.
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents are vulnerable to adversarial inputs that induce attacker-specified malicious behaviors, commonly referred to as jailbreaking. Existing optimization-based jailbreak attacks primarily employ first-order (FO) methods that leverage gradient information or zeroth-order (ZO) methods that rely on function-value feedback. title: ReTRACE: Feedback-Guided LLM Agent in a Chemistry Harness for Retrosynthesis Planning
authors: Jinxiang Xie, Yijian Zhang, Qingyuan Yi et al.
abstract: Computer-aided retrosynthesis has advanced through single-step prediction, tree search and route scoring, but complex targets still require judgement over the whole route, where stereochemistry, functional-group compatibility, cost and greenness interact. Here we present \textbf{\mbox{ReTRACE}} (\textbf{RE}trosynthesis with \textbf{T}ool-orchestrated \textbf{R}easoning \textbf{A}nd \textbf{C}ontext-aware \textbf{E}vidence), an agent that places a large language model (LLM) in a chemistry harness

title: Can LLM Agents Resolve Service Failures? Simulating Multi-Turn Complaint Handling under Information Asymmetry
authors: Wailing Ng, Mengze Hong, Chen Jason Zhang et al.
abstract: LLM agents are widely adopted in service chatbots for rule-guided support and information access, yet emotionally demanding complaint handling still relies heavily on human agents. We introduce ServiceBench, to our knowledge the first benchmark dedicated to complaint handling, with 2,500 scenarios spanning 184 complaint categories and five service industries. title: DiffuPlan: Editable Planning State for Diffusion Language Model Agents
authors: Qisheng Zhou, Zhen Xiong, Qiaoyu Tan
abstract: Diffusion language models (dLLMs) are emerging as an alternative to autoregressive (AR) language models, yet dLLM agents largely inherit an interaction protocol designed for AR generation: once intermediate state is written, later observations can only be incorporated by appending more text. title: Can AI agents make law? Evaluating AI legal relevance and creativity
authors: Benjamin Ricaud, Artem Galushko
abstract: Large language models, the artificial intelligence (AI) systems behind modern chatbots, are trained on vast amounts of legal text, but can they build on it to write law for situations that text never anticipated? In this study, we analyse AI agents' ability to draft a hypothetical "Constitution" for a "community of AI agents". title: Selm: Self-Evolving Library Management for Multi-Skill Agent Optimization
authors: Mengxi Hu, Yuxuan Hu, Jinbo Su et al.
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly use skills as a lightweight way to acquire task-specific knowledge. Recent work enables skills to evolve from task trajectories. title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
authors: Shihao Weng, Longtian Wang, Yang Feng et al.
abstract: Software quality has long rested on specifications that state what code must do, and on testing and verification that check that the code does it. Agentic systems change this foundation: they replace parts of their logic, such as choosing the next tool, judging whether an action is allowed, or writing code to run, with calls to a large language model (LLM). title: HABIT-Bench: Evaluating Habit Induction from Longitudinal Weak Evidence in Agent Memory
authors: Junming Zhang, Rubin Wei, Xu Cheng et al.
abstract: In long-term interactions with large language model (LLM) agents, users reveal habits through their choices and actions. These habits capture implicit user information that agents must infer across conversations. However, individual observations may provide only partial evidence about a habit or when it applies. title: Modeling Discourse Profiles in Climate Misinformation Discourse
authors: Ge Gao, Zhengyang Shan, Bryan A. Plummer et al.
abstract: Prior work on climate misinformation detection typically classifies individual comments or claims using text alone. This framing overlooks a key property of online climate discourse: misinformation is often produced, reinforced, and sustained through recurring rhetorical patterns that reappear across comments and threads. title: Write Once, Check Many: Reusable Ledgers for Post-Hoc Policy Compliance Auditing of Agent Trajectories
authors: Ashwin Nagarajan, Gursimran Panesar, Alicia Yang et al.
abstract: Auditing LLM agents against policies is critical to ensure safety but requires rereading long trajectories once per policy. Can we instead record each trajectory once and reuse that record for policies not known in advance? We propose write once, check many, a framework in which a writer model converts each agent trajectory into a policy-independent ledger of the agent's actions and outcomes. title: MELD: Recursive Self-Improvement via Hierarchical Coordination for Multi-Agent Scientific Discovery
authors: Sizhe Tang, Zuyuan Zhang, Zeyu Fang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent scientific discovery with large language models raises a coupled learning problem: research assignments determine both which experiments are pursued and the experiences from which agents adapt. We introduce MELD, a unified hierarchical test-time training framework that jointly adapts a team-level Coordinator policy and agent-level individual Scientist policies within a single discovery process. title: Hippo: Training-Free Agent Self-Evolution via Hippocampal Replay
authors: Yutong Song, Jiang Wu, Yuxuan Ren et al.
abstract: Motivated by recursive self-improvement (RSI), we study how LLM agents can learn through external memory without updating model parameters. Extracting useful experience from a single attempt is difficult: flawed reasoning can produce success, while poor execution can obscure a sound strategy. title: Ask Less, Ask Better: Allocating User Attention in Proactive LLM Agents with Interruption Budgets
authors: Xuanming Zhang, Amir H. Rezaeian, Miguel Ballesteros et al.
abstract: LLM agents can ask clarifying questions to complete tasks, but answering each question demands users' time and effort. Existing evaluations typically measure this burden by counting questions, treating necessary and avoidable questions equally. We propose an evaluation protocol that distinguishes how often agents ask from how well they ask. title: Bridging Exploration and Persona: Information-Directed Dueling for Test-Time Agent Personalization
authors: Jie Mao, Pingchen Lu, Xiangyi Wang et al.
abstract: Effective test-time personalization requires LLM agents to adapt to query-dependent user preferences from lightweight interaction. We study persona selection with binary comparisons between candidate responses as the online signal. We present ID-TAP, a scalable, IDS-inspired neural dueling-bandit framework for large discrete persona spaces. title: Train Locally, Learn Together: Distributed Multi-Agent Training via ADMM
authors: Yiwei Chen, Changsheng Wang, Yicheng Lang et al.
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) can outperform individual language-model agents by combining specialized roles, diverse reasoning processes, and collaborative decision-making. However, collaborative MAS training is typically centralized, requiring a common trainer to aggregate role-local trajectories and learning signals and maintain model and optimization states. title: Muse Glimmer 30B: An On-Device Agentic Model
authors: Arash Ebrahim Abtahizadeh, Muna Aghamelu, Adil Ahmed et al.
abstract: We introduce Muse Glimmer, an open-source 30B parameter causal language model with perception encoder, purpose-built for autonomous agentic tasks on consumer hardware. Muse Glimmer integrates multi-step reasoning, reliable tool use and failure recovery into a single model that runs locally on consumer devices without requiring cloud infrastructure. title: When LLM-Generated Refactorings Ripple: An Empirical Study of Repository Adoption Readiness
authors: Muhammad Waseem, Aakash Ahmad, Pekka Abrahamsson
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to refactor source files, but file-local evaluations do not reveal changes to contracts, dependencies, or caller assumptions affecting repository adoption. To address this gap, we conduct 1,500 generation attempts across 150 production files from 15 open-source Java repositories, five LLM configurations, and two dependency-aware generation conditions: single-prompt refactoring and LangGraph-based multi-agent refactoring. title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
authors: Ali Ansari, Farhana Ferdousi Liza
abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. title: Scene-Adaptive VLA: Efficient Autonomous Driving via Dynamic Layer Routing
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan et al.
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
authors: Yifei Zhao, Fanyu Zhao, Han Zhang et al.
abstract: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
authors: Mankeerat Sidhu, Gangmuk Lim, Hetarth Chopra et al.
abstract: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. title: AdamPM: Memory-Efficient LLM Optimization via Moment Pooling
authors: Xiaowei Ji, Lishan Xu, Jianing An et al.
abstract: Adam is widely used for training large language models (LLMs) owing to its strong optimization performance and training stability, but its element-wise estimation for the first and second moments incur substantial memory overhead. Although numerous memory-efficient optimizers have been proposed, many incur additional computational overhead or require additional tuning of hyperparameters. title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
authors: unsu Kim, Naeun Kim, Dongyoon Han et al.
abstract: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. title: Defending Against Dormant Poisoning Attacks Across Language and Multimodal Agents
authors: Wonjun Lee, Vaidehi Patil, Zaid Khan et al.
abstract: Recent work shows that attackers can implant dormant malicious behaviors that remain hidden at release but emerge after benign fine-tuning. As foundation models are used as agents, whether dormant poisoning extends to harmful agent actions and multimodal settings remains unclear. We show two agentic risks: (1) harmful behaviors activated by benign fine-tuning can extend to unseen actions; (2) multiple harmful behaviors can coexist and be jointly activated by benign downstream fine-tuning. authors: Khushbu Pahwa, Yubin Ge, Daniele Bonadiman et al.
abstract: LLM code agents increasingly ship code with little oversight, yet defenders trained on static vulnerability datasets fall behind adapting adversaries. authors: Yuan-Chao Li, Yin-Long Liu, Liu He et al.
abstract: Alzheimer's Disease (AD) detection from speech benefits from both paralinguistic and linguistic cues, yet model training is frequently constrained by limited data. Fine-tuning a large pretrained speech encoder can easily overfit, while a frozen probe leaves the encoder's task-relevant knowledge underutilized. title: First-Order LoRA Training with Phone NPUs
authors: Xu Zheng, Wei Cheng, Zhuomin Chen et al.
abstract: On-device fine-tuning lets a large language model (LLM) learn from its user's private data without uploading it. Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces the trainable parameters, but each first-order training step still multiplies by the frozen base-model weights during the forward pass, activation recomputation, and input-gradient computation. title: Medical Fine-Tuning Reshapes, Not Reduces, Patient-Facing AI Risk: A Rubric-Based, LLM-Judge Evaluation Framework
authors: Savan Doshi
abstract: Patient-facing medical question answering with large language models (LLMs) is moving from research demonstrations to production deployments, yet evaluation remains anchored on factual correctness. Factuality is necessary but not sufficient: a response can be factually grounded and still issue a directive that, if acted on, would harm the patient. title: Safety Kernel: Mechanistic Alignment for Cross-Lingual Defense in LLMs
authors: Chengyu Xie, Fei Shen, Shuyi Miao et al.
abstract: The safety capabilities of large language models (LLMs) are highly uneven across different languages, often allowing cross-lingual attacks to bypass safety guardrails. Existing alignment methods predominantly rely on external alignment signals and provide limited insight into underlying neuron-level mechanisms, making it difficult to provide a unified internal target for cross-lingual safety interventions. authors: Giuseppe Giaimis, Sergei Katkov, Muhammad Azfar Yaqub et al.
abstract: Automatic Speech recognition (ASR) struggles with Pathological speech due to persistent speaker-specific mismatch. In clinical and accessibility scenarios, only limited target-speaker data is typically available, making full model retraining impractical.
